commentary: Aquinas reads this opening chapter as the hinge of the whole treatise: having already set aside accidental being and being-as-truth from the science's main business, Aristotle now turns to being-in-itself, and Aquinas shows that this science really reduces to the study of substance. Among the ten categories, substance alone is what "being" means without qualification. When we ask what quality or size something has, we answer with color or measurement; but when we ask what a thing is, we answer with a substance-word, man or god, never with white or three-cubits-long. Every other category is called "being" only derivatively, because it belongs to some substance. Aquinas draws out three respects in which substance is first: in time, since no accident can exist without some substance, though a substance can exist stripped of any particular accident; in definition, because an accident's account must include its subject, the way "snub" includes "nose"; and in knowledge, because we say we truly know something only when we grasp what it is, not merely its quantity or location. Aquinas then notes how Aristotle ties this to the history of philosophy: the ancient and perennial question "what is being?" has always really been the question "what is substance?"—those who argued for one principle or many, finite or infinite, were all disputing about substances without knowing it. This is why the inquiry of the entire book must concentrate almost exclusively on substance.

Aquinas treats this chapter as a survey of received opinion, gathered before any rigorous determination is attempted, so that the inquiry can start from what is least controversial. Bodies are the most obvious substances: animals, plants, the elements, and things composed from them, up through the heavenly bodies. But thinkers disagree once one goes further. Some held that the boundaries of a body—surface, line, point, unit—are more truly substance than the body itself, on the assumption that what is simpler and prior is more real. Plato went further still, positing two orders of separate substance beyond sensible bodies: the Forms and the objects of mathematics, added to sensible substance as a third kind. Speusippus multiplied kinds of substance even more, deriving from a first "One" separate principles for number, for magnitude, and for soul, each functioning as its own independent order of substance. Still others collapsed Plato's distinction between Forms and numbers, treating them as one nature, from which lines and surfaces and eventually the heavens and sensible bodies proceed in a descending series. Aquinas notes that Aristotle withholds judgment on all of this for now, promising later to determine which claims are sound and whether anything exists apart from sensible substance. But he insists that any such judgment presupposes first sketching what sensible substance itself is, since this is the one point everyone concedes, and the natural starting place for the inquiry that follows.

Aquinas identifies four things commonly called substance: essence, universal, genus, and subject or substratum, and he explains why Aristotle begins with the subject, since what most literally underlies everything else seems substance in the fullest sense. This subject itself divides three ways: matter, form, and the composite of both, related not as species under a genus but analogically, by priority and posteriority. Aquinas walks through the reasoning that form outranks matter, since matter is mere potency while form is act, and act is naturally and even temporally prior to potency; and since form outranks matter, it likewise outranks the composite, which depends on both. Yet a serious complication arises: strip away every quantity, quality, and accident from a sensible body, and matter alone seems to remain, tempting the conclusion that matter alone is truly substance. Aquinas explains that the ancients who reasoned this way were misled by their ignorance of substantial form, having no concept beyond the sensible accidents; he shows why the conclusion fails regardless, since substance properly requires two marks, separability and being a determinate "this," and matter possesses neither on its own, since of itself it is pure potency, becoming actual and determinate only through form. Form, and the composite it informs, are therefore the better candidates for substance. Aquinas notes that Aristotle sets the composite aside for now as evidently posterior and knowable enough, and turns to the far more perplexing question of form, proceeding deliberately from what is better known to us toward what is better known by nature.

Here Aquinas follows Aristotle's investigation of essence, what a thing is said to be strictly through itself and not accidentally. Being white is not the essence of "surface," since white and surface have different accounts; nor is "white surface" the essence of surface, since the term surface would then reappear redundantly within its own definition. A genuine statement of essence expresses a thing's meaning without repeating the term itself and without smuggling in anything foreign to it. This raises the question whether things named by the other categories, or accidental compounds like "white man" or the example of "cloak," have essences and definitions in the same sense substances do. Aquinas lays out the resolution taking shape: strictly and primarily, essence and definition belong only to substance, because only there does the answer to "what is it" name something self-subsistent; but in an extended, secondary sense, an accident can be said to have an essence insofar as its account is referred back to some substance, much as "medicinal" is said of a patient's body, a treatment, and an instrument, not univocally, and not by mere chance equivocation, but by relation to one thing, the art of medicine. Aquinas stresses that this is the same pattern by which "being" itself applies primarily to substance and only derivatively, through a kind of proportional likeness, to quantity, quality, and the rest—so essence, like being, has a primary home in substance and a borrowed, dependent sense everywhere else.

Aquinas takes up the harder case of compound terms such as "snub," which cannot be defined without naming their subject. Concavity can be defined without mentioning nose, but snubness cannot, since snubness simply is concavity found specifically in a nose—nose belongs to its very account, not as an accidental addition the way whiteness attaches to Callias. This produces an apparent dilemma: if "snub nose" means nothing but "concave nose," then to define snub nose would be to say "nose" twice over, since concave already implies nose, threatening either absurdity or an infinite regress of repeated terms. Aquinas explains how Aristotle resolves this without abandoning the deeper point already reached: essence and definition belong properly and without qualification to substance alone; but in a secondary, dependent way they can be granted to composite accidents like snubness, provided one recognizes that such an attribute's very account requires its subject, whether that subject appears openly, as in the concrete term "snub," or is folded in, as in the abstract term "snubness," rightly defined as concavity of a nose. Aquinas draws the wider lesson: attributes that inhere in a determinate subject by their own nature, and not merely by accident, cannot be understood or even named apart from that subject, unlike a purely accidental union such as "white man." The upshot, which Aquinas takes as settled for the rest of the book, is that essence and definition in the full and primary sense belong to substances alone, and to everything else only in a diminished, borrowed way.

Aquinas presents Aristotle's inquiry into whether a thing is identical with its own essence. In things said strictly through themselves—substances existing in their own right—thing and essence must be the same, not by accident but according to their very account. Aquinas reconstructs the argument: were a thing's essence something other than the thing, that essence would itself require a further essence, and so on without end, and knowledge itself would become impossible, since to know a thing just is to know its essence; sever the two and neither remains either knowable or, in a sense, real. Aquinas is careful to note that this reasoning is aimed directly at Plato's separately existing Forms: sensible substances need no separate Idea standing behind them to secure their being or their intelligibility, since each already possesses its essence intrinsically and identically with itself. Merely accidental unities, by contrast, like "white man," are not simply identical with their essence, since such a composite includes something, whiteness, foreign to the subject's own nature. Aquinas adds an important refinement often overlooked: even within genuine substances, the abstract essence-term is not wholly the same as the concrete thing—"humanity" signifies only the essential principles, excluding every accident, while "man" signifies the whole subject, in which accidents also inhere; humanity signifies as a part, man as the whole. Only where no accidents exist at all, as in God, do the abstract and the concrete coincide without remainder.

Aquinas walks through Aristotle's threefold division of coming-to-be—by nature, by art, and by chance or spontaneity—and the three elements every generation requires: an agent, a matter from which (the underlying subject, not the mere privation), and a product, which may fall under any category though it belongs most properly to substance. In natural generation, matter, the operative form present in the begetting agent, and the specific form actually produced in the offspring are all called "nature," though in different senses: matter as the underlying substrate, the engendered form as the term toward which the process moves, and the parent's own form as the active principle, specifically alike to what it produces, though numerically distinct, since man begets man but not the very same man. Aquinas highlights Aristotle's analogy from medicine: the physician reasons backward from the form of health he intends, through a chain of intermediate steps, until reaching some immediate action he can himself perform, such as inducing warmth by rubbing; production is simply this same reasoning reversed, moving forward from that starting action to the intended form. Aquinas underscores that everything produced, by nature or art alike, requires matter genuinely capable both of being and of not-being. He also notes the precise way things are named from what they come from: a healed man is called simply "man," not "the sick one," and a statue is called "golden" rather than "gold," because coming-to-be involves the real transformation of a substrate, not the mere persistence of unchanged material with a shape added.

Aquinas treats this chapter as delivering Aristotle's decisive blow against Plato's separated Forms as causes of generation. Since production requires matter, agent, and product, the agent does not, strictly speaking, make the matter, which already pre-exists, nor does it, strictly, make the form: when a bronze sphere is produced, the sphere-shape is said to "come to be" only incidentally, because what is truly generated is the composite, this bronze now made spherical. Aquinas reconstructs the proof: were the agent required to make the form as such, that form would itself need to arise from some further matter, making the form itself composite of matter and form, and generating an endless regress. Hence only the composite of form and matter is strictly generated; the form or essence is not brought into being at all but is "drawn out" from matter's own potency. From this, Aquinas explains, Aristotle concludes that no separately existing universal sphere, house, or man need be posited to explain generation, since the begetter is always itself a concrete individual producing another concrete individual like itself in kind—man begets man, and even the anomalous case of a mule shows the seed's inherent formative power transmitting the nearest attainable likeness. Aquinas stresses that this removes the Platonic need for a Form serving either as an active generating cause or as a separate exemplar-pattern to be imitated, since the individual agent's own form, already present in matter, is entirely sufficient to explain both the production and the specific likeness of what is produced.

Aquinas explains why some things, like health, can arise either through art or spontaneously by chance, while others, like a house, arise only through art. The difference lies in the matter: some matter contains within itself a principle able to move itself toward the relevant form, as the human body possesses an inherent capacity for healing, so that health can sometimes occur "by chance," through mere incidental warming, without any physician's intention; other matter, such as stone and timber, has no such internal motive principle and can be brought to its form only by an external agent possessing the relevant skill. Aquinas notes the parallel Aristotle draws with natural generation: seed carries the form potentially and operates much like an artisan's skill, which is why some living things reproducible from seed can, on ancient biological assumptions, also arise spontaneously from suitably disposed matter, while others require the parent animal itself. Aquinas draws out the chapter's central conclusion, comparing it to a syllogism: just as every syllogism ultimately proceeds from and is resolved into some account of what a thing is, so every process of production ultimately starts from and is explained by substance, that is, by the essential form toward which the process tends. He adds that this same pattern, proved first for substance, extends analogously to quality and quantity, though with an important asymmetry: substantial generation strictly requires that another actual substance already exist to produce it, whereas a quality or quantity need only pre-exist potentially in the substance undergoing change.

Aquinas treats this long chapter as resolving whether the parts into which a definition analyzes must themselves belong to the definition of the whole. He notes the puzzle's two pulling examples: a circle's definition omits any definition of its segments, yet a syllable's definition includes the definition of its letters, though a circle divides into segments just as a syllable divides into letters. A related difficulty concerns priority: parts like the acute angle within a right angle, or a finger within an animal, seem prior to their wholes, since the whole is explained through them, yet a finger cannot exist, except equivocally, once severed from a living body, suggesting the whole is prior instead. Aquinas explains Aristotle's resolution through a crucial distinction of senses of "part." Some parts belong to a thing's matter, such as the bronze constituting a statue, or flesh and bone materially constituting a man; other parts belong properly to the form or intelligible account, such as the letters that constitute what it is to be a syllable. Only these latter, formal parts belong in a genuine definition, since definition concerns the universal species and not material individuation—this is why the material segments of this or that particular circle are excluded from the definition of circle-as-such, while letters, being constitutive of a syllable's very nature, are included. Aquinas illustrates the principle through the soul, which as form is prior to the body's organs; a severed finger, lacking the soul that made it functionally a finger, is a finger in name only.

Aquinas presents Aristotle here closing a gap left open by the previous chapter: which parts belong to form, and so to definition, and which belong only to the concrete composite? Where a form clearly occurs in different kinds of matter, as a circle can be bronze, wood, or stone, it is obvious that this particular matter is no part of the circle's essence. But where a form is always found embedded in one determinate matter, as man is always found in flesh and bone, judgment is harder, and Aquinas notes that some thinkers wrongly concluded, on the model of the circle, that flesh and bone must equally be excluded from man's essence, reducing definitions ultimately to bare numbers, since stripping continuous extension from geometric figures leaves only units. Aquinas details Aristotle's refutation: this reduction absurdly collapses distinct kinds into one, since a triangle, a syllogism, and a body all "share" the number three without being the same kind of thing; and it is simply false that natural definitions can dispense with matter altogether. Unlike a circle, an animal is essentially something sensible, undefinable without reference to motion and therefore to properly disposed bodily parts—a hand counts as a hand only while alive and capable of its function—which is why the comparison some drew between animal and circle fails. Aquinas concludes that natural species genuinely include a kind of matter, called sensible matter, within their definition, and mathematical objects include an analogous intelligible matter, continuous extension, refuting any attempt to strip matter from either kind of definition.

Aquinas explains the puzzle Aristotle takes up here: why is a definition built from genus and differentiae, such as "two-footed animal," one single formula rather than a mere list of separate terms? Unlike a purely accidental unity such as "pale man," where the two terms do not intrinsically belong together, genus and differentia must combine into a genuine unity, and this is puzzling especially since a genus can seemingly be divided by many differentiae in succession. Aquinas traces Aristotle's solution through the method of division: a correct definition results only when each differentia divides the one before it by a further differentia proper to that very respect—footed animal, for instance, correctly divided not into feathered and featherless, an accidental cut, but into cloven-footed and non-cloven, a division intrinsic to footedness itself. When division proceeds this way, every earlier and more generic differentia is effectively contained already within the last, most specific one, so that spelling out the whole chain in words is really only unpacking, redundantly, what the final differentia alone already says. The genuine definition, therefore, is constituted strictly by this last differentia, which turns out to be identical with the thing's very form and substance; nothing is added by repeating the earlier terms once it is reached. Aquinas notes that this is why reordering a properly constructed definition exposes redundancy at once, and why there is, properly speaking, no temporal or logical succession among a substance's differentiae, only a nested unity that culminates in one final, defining differentia.

Aquinas turns to whether universals, as the Platonists held, can themselves be substances. He carefully distinguishes two senses of "universal": the common nature itself, such as animal or man, which does signify substance when predicated of what a thing is, and that same nature considered precisely as universal, that is, as one thing shared by many—and it is only in this second sense that Aristotle denies it is substance. Aquinas lays out the arguments in turn: a thing's substance is proper to it and belongs to nothing else, but a universal by definition is common to many, so it cannot be the substance of all of them together, since then all would collapse into one, nor of any single one alone, since it belongs equally to the rest. Substance, moreover, is what is never said of a subject, while a universal is always predicated of some subject. A further, more technical argument, which Aquinas explains with care, holds that no substance can be composed of substances actually present within it, since two things actually distinct are never thereby made into one actual thing—only what is merely potentially two can become actually one; here Aquinas credits Democritus with seeing the principle correctly, even though he wrongly concluded that magnitudes must therefore be indivisible. Since universals are not substances, and no substance is composed of already-actual substances, Aquinas notes that Aristotle leaves a real difficulty hanging: if no substance can be composite in either of these ways, none seems definable at all, a knot Aristotle only unties later, by showing that substance is composed of substances potentially, not actually.

Aquinas shows how Aristotle presses the previous chapter's conclusion directly against Platonists who make Forms separately subsisting substances while also holding that each Form's definition is composed of genus and differentia. If "animal" is one and the same nature present in both a separately existing Man-itself and Horse-itself, Aquinas explains, then either it is numerically one and the same thing in both, which is impossible, since one undivided thing cannot exist wholly within several separately subsisting things at once, and would also have to bear contrary differentiae, such as two-footed and many-footed, simultaneously; or else it is different in each species, in which case there would be as many distinct "animals" as there are kinds, and each of those, in turn, would need its own participation in some prior Animal-itself, launching a vicious regress with no coherent account of how the levels relate. Aquinas notes that Aristotle presses the point further by comparing genus to individual sensible things rather than merely to species, since the gap the Platonists must bridge is even wider there, making the same absurdities still more severe. The chapter's conclusion, Aquinas stresses, is unqualified: there simply are no separately subsisting Forms of sensible things of the kind the Platonists proposed, because the theory cannot satisfy its own basic requirement—one single nature genuinely and coherently shared, without contradiction, across several distinct individuals.

Aquinas explains Aristotle's demonstration that Platonic Ideas, precisely because they are conceived as separately subsisting individuals, cannot after all be defined—undermining the very purpose for which Plato introduced them, namely to secure fixed objects for definition and demonstration, which changeable sensible things cannot supply. First, individual sensible substances cannot properly be defined or demonstrated about, because their matter is genuinely capable of both being and not-being, making them corruptible; once they pass from the senses through which they are known, no account can reliably track them, whereas definition and demonstration require necessary, unchanging objects. Since a Platonic Idea, however eternal, is still conceived as an individual "this," Aquinas shows it suffers an analogous defect: any definitional formula must be built from several terms, and each term, to be intelligible at all, must be common to more than one thing, since a definition using only names peculiar to a single individual explains nothing genuinely. But then whatever definition is assigned to one Idea will necessarily apply equally to whatever those constituent common terms name elsewhere, destroying the Idea's claimed uniqueness, and even implying, absurdly, that the constituent terms, such as "animal" and "two-footed," are themselves prior to and separable from the supposedly primary Idea of man. Aquinas notes that Aristotle extends the same reasoning even to genuinely unique eternal individuals like the sun: defining the sun by accidental features such as circling the earth or being hidden at night is illegitimate, since the sun would remain the sun even if these features were removed.

Aquinas explains this chapter's two main arguments. First, Aristotle shows that most things ordinarily called substances—the bodily parts of animals, and even earth, air, fire, and water once mixed into a compound—exist only potentially, not actually, so long as they remain genuine parts of a continuous, unified whole; only once physically separated does a former "part" become an actual, independent thing, and at that point it is no longer strictly a part at all. Aquinas notes that living organs come closest to actuality, since they possess an intrinsic principle of motion at their joints, which explains why certain divided animals briefly continue to live, but even these remain merely potential parts as long as the organism stays one continuous natural whole; union produced only by external force or grafting, by contrast, counts as a kind of violence against nature rather than genuine unity. Second, Aristotle argues that neither "being" nor "unity"—nor "principle," "element," or "cause"—can itself be the substance of anything, since substance belongs properly only to the individual thing possessing it, and what is truly one, unlike what is merely common, cannot exist simultaneously in many places at once. Aquinas closes by explaining Aristotle's balanced verdict on Plato: right in recognizing that if common natures were substances they would have to exist separately, since substance is by nature self-subsistent, but wrong in supposing one nature could be both separately subsistent and, at the same time, common to many things at once—an error Aquinas traces to the Platonists having no independent grasp of what immaterial substance actually is, so that they simply projected familiar sensible natures onto a separate, immaterial plane.

Aquinas explains that Aristotle now approaches substance from a fresh starting point, as principle and cause, in order finally to say in reality, and not merely logically, what substance-as-essence is. The method: a genuine "why" question always seeks a cause connecting some predicate to a subject distinct from it—"why does it thunder" reduces to "why is sound produced in the clouds"—while asking why a thing is simply itself is empty, since it presupposes the very identity that would need explaining. Applied to a composite like a house, Aquinas shows, the real question is why these bricks and stones constitute a house at all, and the answer sought is precisely the essence or form, which functions sometimes as an end and sometimes as a first mover, but always as the cause by which matter becomes this determinate thing. Aquinas highlights Aristotle's central insight about composite wholes generally: a syllable is not simply identical with its letters, nor flesh with fire and earth, because something further, beyond the material elements themselves, accounts for their being unified into one thing rather than a mere heap; and this further principle cannot itself be reduced to another element without triggering an endless regress. Aquinas identifies this unifying principle as the thing's substantial form or nature, itself not composed of elements but rather the very cause that binds elements into one determinate substance. With this the book's inquiry closes by locating substance most properly in form, understood as intrinsic formal cause and principle of unity, preparing the way for Book Eight's continued examination of composite substances in light of these same principles.
